chunks.heading: Chapter 11 391
chunks.content:
and effective security training experience, but also dynamically adjust the training content based
on employee feedback and performance to offer personalized learning paths.
Applying LLMs in Cybersecurity 392
By analyzing employee behaviors and responses during training, LLMs can identify employees’
strengths and weaknesses, thereby providing more targeted training content. This personalized
learning experience not only improves employees’ learning efficiency but also helps them better
understand and master security knowledge.
Intelligence sharing and collaboration
In the field of intelligence sharing and collaboration in cybersecurity, LLMs play a key role.
Their core capability lies in integrating and analyzing security threat intelligence from multiple
sources. Through deep learning and pattern recognition technologies, LLMs can extract valuable
information from massive amounts of data and identify similarities in security incidents across
different organizations, thereby uncovering common threat patterns and attack trends.
This ability is particularly important when dealing with global security threats, especially
potential cyberattacks against critical infrastructure. Critical infrastructure (such as power grids,
water treatment systems, and traffic control systems) is essential to national security and social
operation. By analyzing historical security data of these infrastructures, LLMs can predict and
identify possible attack vectors, preparing defenses in advance.
Compliance monitoring
In the current context of increasingly strict data protection regulations, LLM technology has
become an important tool for enterprises to ensure compliance. With precise data analysis
capabilities, it helps enterprises monitor and manage data processing activities to meet stringent
legal requirements. In a globalized environment, LLM technology enables enterprises to adapt
to data protection regulations across different countries and regions, providing assurance for
smooth international business operations.
For example, when an Asian company sets up a branch in Europe, it must process personal data in
accordance with the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). LLMs can deeply analyze the
company’s data processing workflows and sensitively identify any behavior that may violate the
GDPR, including unauthorized use of personal data or insecure data processing practices. Through
this advanced monitoring mechanism, enterprises can not only promptly rectify violations but
also prevent potential compliance risks, thus significantly reducing compliance risk. This not only
helps enterprises avoid possible legal sanctions and financial losses but also protects customers’
privacy rights, enhancing the company’s reputation and customer trust.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 11 393
chunks.content:
Chapter 11 393
These examples show that LLMs can strengthen many parts of the security lifecycle, from detection
and investigation to training and compliance. However, the same qualities that make them
useful in security workflows also create new risks. Models that process sensitive data, generate
recommendations, and influence operational decisions must be governed carefully. Before
organizations can rely on LLMs as part of their security architecture, they must also understand
the vulnerabilities, misuse scenarios, and control measures associated with the models themselves.
Managing the security risks of LLMs
LLMs have demonstrated tremendous potential in natural language processing, image recognition,
data analysis, and many other fields due to their powerful data processing capabilities and deep
learning algorithms. However, as with any technological advancement, the application of LLMs
is accompanied by new security challenges and operational risks.
Inherent risks
The inherent risks of LLMs include four aspects: access control vulnerabilities, prompt injection,
content hallucinations, and poisoning of training data.
Access control vulnerabilities
The training and deployment of LLMs typically require massive computational resources, which
are often distributed across different servers and data centers. To ensure efficient operation of
the model, appropriate data access permissions must be provided. However, if access control
mechanisms are not sufficiently strict or have flaws, they can become targets for attackers.
Attackers may exploit these vulnerabilities to gain unauthorized access to sensitive data or even
conduct malicious operations on the model, such as implanting malicious code or tampering with
model parameters, thereby affecting the normal operation and output of the model.
Prompt injection
Prompt injection is a type of attack that exploits vulnerabilities at the model’s input side. Attackers
craft specially designed inputs (i.e., prompts) to induce the model to produce unexpected outputs.
Such attacks may cause the model to leak training data, perform specific operations, or generate
misleading information. For example, an attacker could use prompt injection to induce the
language model to generate text containing sensitive information or to produce malicious code
capable of bypassing security checks.
Applying LLMs in Cybersecurity 394
Content hallucinations and poisoning of training data
Content hallucinations and poisoning of training data are two other major challenges faced by
LLMs. Content hallucination refers to attackers generating specific input samples that cause the
model to make incorrect predictions or classifications. These input samples may appear visually
identical to normal samples but are sufficient to cause a sharp decline in model performance.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 11 393
chunks.content:
Training data poisoning refers to attackers injecting malicious samples into the training data
during the model’s training phase, causing the model to learn incorrect patterns. Once these
patterns are learned by the model and applied to real tasks, the model’s decisions and outputs
may become biased.
These inherent weaknesses become more serious when LLMs are connected to real systems,
users, data stores, and business workflows. At that point, model-level risks begin to overlap
with application security concerns.
Application security risks
The application security risks of LLMs can be categorized into four aspects: data leakage, AI
ethics and morality, prompt jailbreak, and supply chain security.
Data leakage
When LLMs handle sensitive data, improper protection may lead to data leakage. Such data may
include personal privacy information, trade secrets, or state secrets. Data leakage not only causes
serious harm to individuals and enterprises but may also trigger legal action and reputational
loss. Therefore, how to effectively safeguard data security while ensuring model performance is
a key issue that needs to be addressed in the application of LLMs.
AI ethics and morality
The application of LLMs also involves issues of ethics and morality. Since model training typically
relies on large volumes of data, these datasets may contain biased or discriminatory content. If
the model learns and amplifies these biases, it may lead to discriminatory outcomes, such as
unfair scoring of certain groups in fields like recruitment or credit approval. In addition, LLMs
can be used to create false information, such as deepfake technologies, posing serious threats to
social order and public safety.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 11 395
chunks.content:
Chapter 11 395
Prompt jailbreaks
Prompt jailbreak refers to attackers using specific inputs to bypass the model’s security constraints,
thereby accessing or executing unauthorized functions. This method of attack poses a serious
threat to model security. For instance, attackers may use prompt jailbreaks to access the model’s
internal structure or perform specific operations, such as stealing data or implanting malware.
Supply chain security
The supply chain for LLMs may also become a target for attacks. From data collection and model
training to deployment, every step in the supply chain may contain security vulnerabilities.
Attackers might inject malicious code or tamper with model parameters at these stages, thereby
affecting the normal operation of the model. Hence, ensuring the security of the supply chain is
an essential part that cannot be overlooked in LLM applications.
Because these risks span data, access, model behavior, and deployment pipelines, they cannot
be addressed through a single control. Effective mitigation requires layered safeguards across
the full lifecycle of the LLM system.
Counteracting risks
The adversarial risks of LLMs include three aspects: the data lifecycle principle, data noise
addition techniques, and the zero-trust principle for access control.
Data lifecycle principles
To address the security challenges posed by LLMs, the data lifecycle principle should be
followed to ensure that data is properly protected at every stage—collection, storage, processing,
transmission, and destruction. This includes measures such as data encryption, access control,
and auditing to prevent data leakage and misuse.
Data noise addition techniques
Data noise addition technology is an effective countermeasure that injects random noise into
data to reduce its sensitivity and thus improve model security. This approach can increase the
difficulty for attackers to extract useful information from the data without significantly impacting
model performance.
Applying LLMs in Cybersecurity 396
Zero trust principles for access control
The zero trust principle is an important security strategy that assumes that all entities inside
and outside the network are untrusted and therefore requires strict identity verification and
authorization for every access. This principle can effectively prevent unauthorized access and
insider threats, thereby enhancing system security.
Risk management is not only about protecting LLM systems from misuse; it is also about
understanding whether LLMs can help reduce security risks in software itself. One important
area is vulnerability repair, where models are asked to suggest fixes for insecure code. The next
discussion looks at how zero-shot LLMs perform in this setting, and what their results reveal
about both the promise and the limits of using LLMs for automated security remediation.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 11 395
chunks.content:
Evaluating zero-shot vulnerability repair with LLMs
The discussion now narrows from broad security risks to one specific question: can LLMs help
repair vulnerable code without being specially trained for that task? This is an important place
to end the chapter because vulnerability repair brings together several themes covered earlier—
code generation, security testing, prompt design, model reliability, and human oversight. The
following discussion examines a zero-shot vulnerability repair study, beginning with the research
motivation, then moving through the experimental setup, the generation of vulnerable programs,
the effect of prompt design, and finally the reliability of the repair code produced by LLMs.
Research background
After undergoing extensive source code training, LLMs have been used to assist developers in
completing coding tasks, such as translation between different programming languages and
code understanding. Among the many downstream code tasks, development teams and security
teams need to pay special attention to the ability of LLMs to repair code security vulnerabilities.
Traditionally, this process is carried out by security testers who run security tools (such as
Fuzzers or static analyzers), interpret the feedback from these tools, locate problematic code,
and ultimately fix security vulnerabilities in the code.
In practice, an important question arises: Can the “out-of-the-box” LLMs used for code
completion help developers repair security vulnerabilities? In the security field, this capability
of LLMs has three security-oriented characteristics: black box, immediate code LLM capabilities,
and the impact of zero-shot methods on vulnerability repair.
The paper Examining Zero-Shot Vulnerability Repair with LLMs gives us some inspiration from
four aspects:

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 11 397
chunks.content:
Chapter 11 397
• Can existing “out-of-the-box” LLMs generate secure and functionally correct code to
repair security vulnerabilities?
• Does changing the amount of code comment context in a prompt affect the ability of
LLMs to provide repair suggestions?
• What challenges exist when using LLMs to repair code security vulnerabilities in real-
world scenarios?
• How reliable are LLMs in generating repair code?
To answer these questions, the study moves from general interest in LLM-based vulnerability
repair to a structured experimental design. The research approach defines which models were
evaluated, how vulnerable programs were prepared, how prompts were constructed, and how
generated patches were tested for both security and functional correctness.
Research approach
LLM technology is essentially a scalable sequence prediction model; that is, given a prompt
containing a sequence of tokens, the model predicts and outputs the set of “most likely” next
tokens. In code large models, LLMs can be used to accomplish downstream tasks such as writing
function bodies and code comments. Parameters of LLMs such as temperature, top-p, and top-k
are used to fine-tune the diversity and alignment preferences of generated code. This method
has achieved good results in code-assisted generation scenarios.
Researchers at New York University evaluated the performance of several ready-to-use LLMs in
the context of code security vulnerability repair. Figure 11.1 summarizes the basic characteristics
of these LLMs. Among them, the first three models are different versions of the OpenAI’s Codex
model; the 4th and 5th items are different versions of the AI21’s Jurassic-1 model. All the above
models are accessed via API services. The 6th entry, polycoder, is a locally deployed pre-trained
LLM, and the 7th, gpt2-csrc, is a locally trained LLM using a C/C++ code dataset.
Figure 11.1: Basic characteristics of several LLMs
Applying LLMs in Cybersecurity 398
The authors of the paper designed and implemented a complete process for repairing programs
with security vulnerabilities, as shown in Figure 11.2.
Figure 11.2: Automatic program vulnerability repair flowchart
First, the original program with security vulnerabilities is input into a security tool for testing. Then,
CodeQL is used to manage and analyze the program’s source code and vulnerability information.
Next, the program’s source code, comments, and other information are formatted into prompt
content according to a preset prompt template and input to the LLM being evaluated. With the
code prediction capabilities of the LLM, the vulnerabilities are repaired. Finally, the patched
program is subjected to security testing using the same test cases as in the first step to verify
whether the vulnerability has been successfully fixed, and functional validation is simultaneously

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 11 397
chunks.content:
performed to ensure the program runs properly.
With this repair pipeline in place, the next step was to construct vulnerable programs and evaluate
how effectively different models and prompt settings could repair them.
Experimental process
The authors conducted their experiments by constructing an artificially synthesized dataset of
program source code containing vulnerabilities. The experiments were divided into two phases:
the first phase was model parameter scanning in order to identify the appropriate “typical”
parameters for LLMs to generate repair code; the second phase focused on prompts to determine
whether, as “bug context” information increases, different prompt patterns would affect the
quality of repair code generated by black-box LLMs.

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 11 399
chunks.content:
Chapter 11 399
Generation of vulnerable programs
The authors selected two vulnerabilities from the CWE Top 25 list as the targets for their artificially
synthesized programs: CWE-787 (Out-of-bounds Write) and CWE-89 (SQL Injection). Both
are high-impact vulnerabilities on the CWE Top 25 list that could result in data loss/leakage or
privilege escalation. These two vulnerabilities are relatively easy to detect and can be directly
identified in the given code without any additional context.
CWE-787 and CWE-89 are presented at two different levels of abstraction: CWE-787 tends to
occur in low-level languages like C/C++, which allow direct manipulation of memory pointers,
while CWE-89 typically occurs in high-level languages such as Java or Python. This means that
the experiments can assess the vulnerability repair capabilities of LLMs across two different
facets of software development.
To generate a large quantity of functionally unique yet similarly vulnerable programs, LLMs were
used to generate a substantial amount of vulnerable code as the evaluation dataset, following
these steps:
1. Specify vulnerable programs related to CWE-787 and CWE-89 as the opening Prompts
2. Input the prompts into OpenAI’s Codex LLM (using both code-cushman-001 and code-
davinci-001 versions), generating 500 code samples from each
3. Perform unit testing and CodeQL-based analysis on these code samples
4. Use functionally correct yet vulnerable programs as the dataset
Figure 11.3 provides the statistical details of the generated code samples. Among them, there are
388 functionally correct but vulnerable code samples for CWE-787 and 23 for CWE-89.
Figure 11.3: Vulnerable program samples - Table comparing CWE-787 and CWE-89 on generated,
verified, functional and vulnerable counts
Applying LLMs in Cybersecurity 400
After constructing a dataset of programs that were both functional and vulnerable, the researchers
could test the central question of the study: whether ready-to-use LLMs can generate patches
without task-specific training or fine-tuning. This experiment evaluates the models’ zero-shot
repair capability by prompting them with vulnerable programs and then testing whether the
generated code removes the vulnerability while preserving functionality.
Testing LLM Vulnerability Repair
Using the code for 95 CWE-787 and 22 CWE-89 vulnerable programs as prompts, we queried
two LLMs— code-cushman-001 and code-davinci-001 —for vulnerability fix code. Each model
generated 500 code samples at a time, resulting in 47,500 and 11,000 samples for the two
vulnerabilities, respectively. Figure 11.4 illustrates the proportion of successful fixes.
Figure 11.4: Schematic of fix verification proportions
It can be seen that among the 22,034 valid programs for the CWE-787 scenario, 2.2% were fixed,

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 11 399
chunks.content:
and among the 10,796 valid programs for the CWE-89 scenario, 29.6% were fixed. Notably, even
without any additional contextual assumptions, LLMs can generate bug-free code with zero
samples, meaning they can be used for automated vulnerability repairs in downstream tasks.
In addition, the paper’s authors also observed that different LLM parameters have varying impacts
on code fixes, as shown in Figure 11.5 and Figure 11.6. LLMs with higher temperature parameters
perform better for CWE-787 fixes but worse for CWE-89, and vice versa. Therefore, it seems there
is no single temperature parameter that covers all cases. Furthermore, overall, the higher the value
of the top-p parameter, the better the performance. Accordingly, following the recommendations
from Codex’s official documentation, the authors set the temperature to a broad range {0, 0.25,
0.50, 0.75, 1.00} in subsequent experiments, and top-p to a fixed value of 1.0, which reduced
the subsequent evaluation search space by 80%.

chunks.heading: Chapter 11 401
chunks.content:
Chapter 11 401
Figure 11.5: Impact of different LLM parameters on code repair - Two tables compare CWE
787 bug generation for codecushman001 and codedavinci001 models
Figure 11.6: Impact of different LLM parameters on code repair - Two tables compare CWE-89
bug generation for codecushman001 and codedavinci001 models
After establishing that out-of-the-box models can repair some vulnerabilities, the study next
examines whether the amount of context included in the prompt affects the quality of those repairs.
Applying LLMs in Cybersecurity 402
Testing prompt context for vulnerability repair
By increasing the types of prompts (such as adding or reducing the amount of context in comments)
and evaluating a broader range of vulnerability scenarios, the impact of prompt engineering on
vulnerability repair is assessed. The details of the experimental setup are as follows.
Considering that methods using LLMs to generate code samples might implicitly provide clues for
the LLM to generate vulnerability fixes, the experiment adopts a manual construction approach.
Seven typical vulnerability types from the CWE Top 25 were selected, and code samples containing
vulnerabilities were constructed (specifically CWE-79, CWE-125, CWE-20, CWE-416, CWE-476,
CWE-119, CWE-732), forming the basis for further prompt engineering evaluation.
Prompt design for vulnerability repair
To test the role of context more systematically, the researchers designed multiple prompt templates
that provided different levels of information about the vulnerability and the intended fix.
Multiple prompt comment templates were used in the experiments to enhance the context
information of prompts for each vulnerability scenario. Since there are many possible natural
language formulations for vulnerability fixing prompts, the paper refers to user guides from
models like Codex and comment keywords retrieved from Github to design five prompt templates.
These templates varied the amount of context provided to the LLM, ranging from providing no
information (n.h.) to a large amount of comments and hints (c. / c.m.), as detailed in Figure 11.7.
Figure 11.7: Prompt comment templates

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: Chapter 11 403
chunks.content:
Chapter 11 403 Based on the above experimental evaluation results, there are significant performance differences between different prompt templates, vulnerability scenarios, and LLMs. In some cases (such as CWE-20), prompt templates with less context information (n.h., s.1, s.2) perform better than those with richer context (c. and c.m.). However, in some scenarios (such as CWE-79 and CWE- 732), the opposite is true. Experimental results are shown in Figure 11.8. Figure 11.8: Experimental results for different prompt templates It is worth noting that prompt templates constructed by providing contextual information may not supply enough information to generate code that successfully passes functional tests. That is, the generated patch code may pass security tests but fail functional tests. The authors illustrate this with an example code sample for CWE-79 (XSS vulnerability): The following is the vulnerable source code: bp = Blueprint('hello', __name__) @bp.route("hello/") def hello(username): return "

Hello, %s!

" % username The following is the prompt constructed with the n.h. template: @bp.route("hello/") def hello(username): return "Hello, %s!" % escape(username) Although the username variable is filtered to fix the XSS vulnerability, since the returned string does not contain the

tag, the code fails the functional test. Applying LLMs in Cybersecurity 404 In contrast, the following is a piece of vulnerable code where sufficient context is provided in comments, allowing the LLM to generate a fix that passes both functional and security tests: @bp.route("hello/") def hello(username): # BUG: Reflected server-side cross-site scripting # return "

Hello, %s!

" % username

chunks.title: llmsformodernsoftwaredeliveryanddevops
chunks.heading: # FIXED:
chunks.content:
# FIXED: return "

Hello, %s!

" % escape(username) These prompt experiments show that repair success depends not only on whether a generated patch removes a vulnerability, but also on whether it preserves the intended behavior of the original program. The next step is therefore to evaluate reliability more broadly by comparing successful repairs across synthesized vulnerable programs, manually written examples, and real-world CVE samples. Assessing the reliability of generated repair code The authors evaluated 117 simple synthesized programs containing two types of CWE vulnerabilities (95 CWE-787, 22 CWE-89). The LLM generated 58,500 possible patches, of which 3,688 successfully completed repairs. Next, 7 manually written vulnerable programs containing CWE vulnerabilities were prepared; the LLM generated a total of 10,000 possible patches, among which 2,796 achieved successful repair (covering 100% of the 7 programs). In addition, the authors also used 12 real-world CVE program samples, for which the LLM generated 19,600 patches, 982 of which fixed the vulnerabilities. Overall, detailed prompts can guide the LLM to generate repair patch code more effectively. LLMs perform best when only short, local repair code is needed, while their performance declines in cases requiring complex context. Furthermore, considering the fact that 100% of the synthesized and manually written vulnerable programs were convincingly fixed, we are confident in the quality of code generated by LLMs for repairing security vulnerabilities. However, based on qualitative analysis results from real-world scenarios (CVE program samples), LLMs are still not sufficient to replace existing manual analysis and semi-automatic repair tools. For example, repairs based on LLMs are currently limited to localized positions within a single file, etc.

chunks.heading: Chapter 11 405
chunks.content:
Chapter 11 405
Summary
In this chapter, you learned how LLMs can be applied in security scenarios, including anomaly
detection, threat identification, phishing and malware analysis, intrusion detection, compliance
monitoring, and vulnerability repair. You also explored the challenges and risks of using LLMs
in security, along with methods for mitigating those risks and improving the reliability of LLM-
based security workflows.
As this is the final chapter, you should now have a broad understanding of how LLMs can be applied
across the software delivery lifecycle—from DevOps, testing, programming, project management,
and operations to security. After reading this book, readers should be able to identify practical
LLM use cases in their own work, evaluate where these models add value, understand their
limitations, and begin designing real-world workflows that combine LLMs with engineering,
operational, and business systems.
